chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that only the *trailing* run of one digest counts, using events `_fail(2, digest="a"), _fail(3, digest="b"), _fail(4, digest="b")`. The longest run of any single digest here is 2 (`"b"`), which is below the default threshold of 3, so the assertion `_repeats(evs) == []` also holds for an implementation that takes the *maximum* run over the whole history instead of the trailing run. To actually distinguish the two, the non-trailing digest would have to reach the threshold, e.g. `a, a, a, b, b` (trailing run 2 → no warning, max run 3 → the buggy implementation warns). As written the test passes either way.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repeated_failure.py::test_only_the_trailing_run_of_one_digest_counts

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims a failure with a missing digest breaks the streak, using `_fail(2, digest="aaaa"), _fail(3, digest=""), _fail(4, digest="aaaa")`. Whether the implementation treats the empty-digest event as a break (leaving one trailing `"aaaa"`) or simply skips/ignores it (leaving two consecutive `"aaaa"`), the resulting count is at most 2, which is under the default threshold of 3, so `_repeats(evs) == []` in both cases. The test would only bite if the two same-digest failures straddling the empty one reached the threshold, e.g. `aaaa, aaaa, "", aaaa` (break → 1, skip → 3 → warning). As written it cannot fail.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repeated_failure.py::test_a_failure_with_no_digest_breaks_the_streak

chunk_findings.detail: The gate command in `_setup` is constant (`python -c "print(chr(98)*3); sys.exit(1)"`), so its output digest is `"bbb"` regardless of the working tree. After three such failures the detector blocks the fourth run. The test then writes `a.py` and expects the next run to return `FAIL` (allowed). But the stated criterion is “N consecutive failures of one gate with the same output digest”; the output digest is still `"bbb"`, so a digest-only detector still sees three identical failures and should return `REFUSED` again. The test therefore requires the detector to key on the tree (or on a `tree_sha` that the evidence contract in the intent does not list). If the implementation follows the intent, this test fails on its last line; if it passes, the detector is enforcing an undocumented tree condition. Either way the change is inconsistent with the specified behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repeated_failure.py::test_block_refuses_a_gate_rerun_on_an_unchanged_tree_with_the_evidence

chunk_findings.detail: The events are three identical failures with digest `a` followed by two with `b`. The test asserts no `repeated_failure` finding. But the first three are exactly “N identical failures” of the same gate with the same output digest, which the acceptance says must trigger the warning. By requiring the run to be the trailing one, the detector silently ignores a completed loop of three identical re-applications: for input `[gate.failed a, gate.failed a, gate.failed a, gate.failed b, gate.failed b]` no doctor note or brief line is produced for the three `a` failures. That contradicts “N identical failures trigger the warning”.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_repeated_failure.py::test_only_the_trailing_run_of_one_digest_counts

chunk_findings.detail: The new refusal forwards the gate's `cwd` unchanged, but for every gate whose `[gate.*].cwd != "worktree"` that value is the empty string — visible in the helper directly above the new function: `return (repo, "") if gdef.cwd != "worktree" else _item_tree(...)`. Run the scenario: a repo-level gate (e.g. a lint/typecheck gate with `cwd` unset) has failed 3× with the same digest under `[loops].on_detect = "block"`, so a `repeated_failure` finding with a non-empty `tree_sha` exists. On the next `ddflow gate run`, line ~292 evaluates `G.tree_fingerprint("")`. An empty path cannot name the repo tree the recorded `tree_sha` was taken from: depending on how `tree_fingerprint` treats it, it either resolves an empty path against the *process* cwd (so an invocation made from the item worktree or any subdirectory fingerprints a different tree than the one the finding recorded, and the `!= f.tree_sha` branch returns `None` — the block silently never fires, and a fix made in the repo does not lift the refusal, contradicting the docstring's "Changing the work lifts the refusal -- the fingerprint is the tree's" and the README's "a different tree lifts it") or it is passed through to a `subprocess`-style `cwd=""`, which raises for the very common non-worktree gate instead of returning a refusal. Everywhere else the empty `cwd` is resolved to the repo root before use; the new probe is the one place it isn't, so the `tree_sha` comparison for non-worktree gates is against the wrong tree (or errors). The fix is to compare against the same resolved directory the gate/recording uses, e.g. `G.tree_fingerprint(cwd or repo)`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py — `_refuse_repeated_failure` / `G.tree_fingerprint(cwd)`

chunk_findings.detail: The test (and therefore the detector it pins down) only evaluates the trailing run of equal digests. Input: `BASE`, then `gate.failed`/`unit_tests`/`output_digest="aaaa"` at seq 2, 3, 4, then `output_digest="bb"` at seq 5 and 6. That log holds three consecutive identical failures of one gate, which the acceptance criterion says must warn, but `_repeats(evs)` is asserted to be `[]`. Any subsequent failure with a different digest (e.g. a flaky/new output) erases the already-observed loop, so `ddflow loops`/`doctor` and the item brief will not surface the re-apply loop the feature exists to catch.
